summary: ORBITONE is an interactive multiplayer space mission design game that turns complex aerospace systems engineering into a collaborative, real-time team challenge. Aligned with the Space Mission Design Game challenge, up to four players step into distinct mission specialist roles—coordinating spacecraft architecture, propulsion, power, communications, orbit selection, and scientific payloads under strict mass, budget, and power limits. Grounded in real NASA open data, every engineering choice triggers cascading trade-offs across the spacecraft, teaching students and aspiring engineers why missions succeed or fail through hands-on experimentation rather than passive facts.
details:
ORBITONE

Every space mission is a team decision.

An interactive multiplayer space mission simulator that makes the engineering trade-offs behind space exploration accessible to everyone.

The Problem

A successful space mission is never designed around one decision. Every subsystem depends on the others.

A more powerful science instrument might collect better data, but it also adds mass, consumes more power and generates more data that must be transmitted back to Earth. A heavier spacecraft could exceed the launch vehicle’s capacity. A power-intensive payload could struggle during periods when the spacecraft is in Earth’s shadow.

These are the kinds of trade-offs that real mission engineers have to work through together.

But for most students, these decisions remain hidden behind equations, technical terminology and textbooks. They rarely get the opportunity to experience how changing one part of a spacecraft can affect the entire mission.

We wanted to change that.

What is ORBITONE?

ORBITONE is a multiplayer space mission design simulator where players work together as a mission control team to plan, build and test a spacecraft.

Instead of simply reading about aerospace engineering, players get to make the decisions themselves, see the consequences and work with their teammates to find solutions.

The experience is built around four stages:

1. Choose a Mission. Build a Team.

Players begin by selecting a mission scenario, with options including Earth Observation, Lunar Reconnaissance and Deep Space Science.

Each player takes responsibility for a different part of the mission:

* Mission Architect: Oversees the overall mission design and makes sure the different subsystems work together.

* Propulsion & Orbit Lead: Handles propulsion choices and orbital requirements.

* Power & Thermal Engineer: Manages energy requirements and thermal constraints.

* Science & Communications Lead: Balances scientific payload capabilities with data collection and communication requirements.

Every role has its own responsibilities, but no player can complete the mission alone.

2. Make the Trade-offs.

This is where the real challenge begins.

Players configure their spacecraft by making decisions about individual subsystems. Each decision updates the mission’s overall parameters in real time.

For example, choosing a higher-resolution science payload may improve scientific return, but it also increases spacecraft mass, power consumption and data requirements.

That decision could affect launch feasibility, battery capacity and communication requirements.

Players must discuss their choices, understand the compromises and find a configuration that works for the entire mission.

3. Run the Mission.

Once the team is satisfied with its design, it can run the mission simulation.

ORBITONE evaluates the spacecraft configuration and shows whether the mission can meet its launch and operational constraints.

Players can see how their design performs across factors such as orbital requirements, power margins and communications.

A mission that looks good on paper might not perform as expected once all the subsystems are considered together.

4. Learn From the Results.

Every mission ends with a post-mission analysis.

Rather than simply showing a success or failure screen, ORBITONE explains what happened and why.

Players can understand which decisions created problems, where they made effective compromises and how they could improve their design.

They can then return to the design stage, make changes and try again.

What Makes ORBITONE Different?

Learning through experience

Players discover aerospace concepts by making decisions and seeing their consequences. They do not need prior knowledge of aerospace engineering to get started.

Collaboration, not competition

Real spacecraft are designed by teams of specialists. ORBITONE reflects this by giving every player a distinct responsibility and making teamwork essential to mission success.

Complex engineering, made accessible

The interface presents technical relationships through intuitive visuals, live mission metrics and simple explanations. Even beginners can understand why a design works or fails.

Built for learning beyond the screen

ORBITONE is designed with schools, student clubs, STEM workshops and hackathons in mind. It gives educators a practical way to introduce aerospace, engineering, problem-solving and systems thinking through a shared experience.

Technology & Implementation

We built ORBITONE as a responsive, browser-based multiplayer application.

Application & Simulation

* Vite

* TypeScript

* Three.js

UI/UX & Testing

* Figma

* Chrome DevTools

* Playwright

NASA Data Integration

* NASA MCP integration

* NASA Open APIs

NASA’s open-data ecosystem provides a foundation for connecting the simulator with real space science and mission-related information.

Feasibility & What’s Next

Within the hackathon timeframe, we developed a playable, responsive multiplayer experience that brings mission planning, subsystem trade-offs and post-mission analysis into one platform.

There is still plenty of room to take ORBITONE further.

Our next priorities include:

* Richer orbital visualisation: More detailed orbital mechanics and spacecraft visualisations to help players understand how their designs behave in space.

* Live space-weather events: Integrating NASA DONKI data to introduce real-world space-weather events as mission challenges, with appropriate effects on spacecraft systems.

* Classroom sandbox: A dedicated mode where teachers can create scenarios, guide student teams and explore engineering concepts at their own pace.

* More mission scenarios: Expanding the simulator with additional destinations, spacecraft configurations and scientific objectives.

Our goal is to make ORBITONE a learning environment where students can experiment, collaborate and develop an appreciation for the engineering behind space exploration.

Because understanding space exploration should not stop at learning how missions work. Students should have the opportunity to experience what it takes to make one work.
